title: Wren and the Tide
premise: Mara Blackwood has spent ten years raising her daughter Wren alone in the coastal town of Salt Hollow, keeping the memory of Eli Vance—the man who left without a word—locked behind the counter of her bookshop. When a clerical error names both Mara and Eli as co-owners of the town's dying orchard, he returns to contest it, and old wounds reopen alongside new evidence that his departure was engineered by Mara's late father to protect a secret about Wren's birth. As they fight the deed through channels the law won't touch, they uncover the truth: Eli never stopped loving her, and Wren deserves the whole story. In the end, they sign the orchard over to the town together, say the rehearsed sentence at last, and choose each other—not because time ran out, but because they finally stopped running from it.
about_author: Ivo Underhill is the pen name of a former tide-chart clerk who spent fifteen years writing love letters for other people before writing any of their own. They live in a converted net shed on the northern coast, where the orchards are stubborn and the tides keep better secrets than most people.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A county clerk's letter arrives naming Mara Blackwood and Eli Vance as joint owners of Blackwood Orchard, a property she thought her father settled years ago. She burns dinner, snaps at Wren, and stares at a name she hasn't spoken aloud in a decade. The emotional beat is dread disguised as irritation—her carefully ordered life cracking open on an ordinary Tuesday.

chapters.title: Salt in the Return Address
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli drives back into Salt Hollow after ten years away, telling himself this is about property, not people. He passes the bookshop twice without stopping and learns from the hardware store gossip that Mara has a daughter. The beat is cowardice curdling into resolve—he'll fix the deed fast and leave before anyone can ask why he really went.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Eli walks into the bookshop and the rehearsed sentence—'I waited'—dies in both their throats. They argue coldly about lawyers while Wren watches from the stacks, recognizing something unspoken. That night Mara finds her father's old ledger with a page torn out. The beat is grief wearing armor; hatred would be easier than what she actually feels.

chapters.title: What the Orchard Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Forced to inspect the orchard together by the county, they walk rows of blighted apple trees and memories surface despite themselves—a first kiss by the well, a promise under the north fence. Eli flinches when Wren mentions her birthday. The beat is reluctant tenderness; the land remembers what they've agreed to forget.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara reconstructs the missing ledger page and finds payments—her father paying someone named Corliss monthly for years after Eli left. Meanwhile Wren, curious about the stranger, asks Eli point-blank if he knew her mother 'before.' The beat is suspicion turning inward: was Eli bought off, or was her father protecting something worse?

chapters.title: Corliss
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli tracks down Ruth Corliss, his former employer, who confesses: Mara's father paid him to run Eli out of town, threatening to reveal a secret about Wren's parentage that would have destroyed them both. Eli took the money and the exile rather than risk it. The beat is shame finally spoken aloud—he wasn't faithless, he was frightened, which is somehow worse.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Confrontation in the closed bookshop after hours: Mara demands the truth, Eli gives it, including what her father knew about Wren's birth and why silence felt like protection. Mara says the rehearsed sentence at last—'I waited'—and then takes it back: 'No. I lived. You owe me more than waiting.' The beat is the climax's emotional detonation; love and fury in the same breath.

chapters.title: High Water
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A storm floods the low road and traps Wren and Eli at the orchard cottage overnight while Mara searches frantically. Wren, furious and curious, makes him tell her everything herself—and decides, with a child's terrible clarity, that she gets a vote. The beat is rising external stakes mirroring internal ones; the family forms in the dark before it dares form in daylight.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The county moves to auction the orchard; the legal route is dead. Mara, Eli, Wren, and half the town—including reformed rival Ruth Corliss—mount a quiet campaign: petitions, a benefit night at the bookshop, testimony about what the orchard means. The beat is justice built by hand; belonging proven not by blood or paper but by who shows up.

chapters.title: Grafting Season
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The town wins the orchard; Mara and Eli sign it over together, then plant a new tree where the torn page used to be buried. On the porch, Eli says his own rehearsed sentence—'I came back'—and Mara answers with the present tense at last. Wren falls asleep between them. The beat is resolution without erasure: the past acknowledged, grafted onto something still growing.
